title: Clinical Characteristics of Cholinergic Urticaria in Korea
author: Kim et al.
passage: A clinical cohort describes cholinergic urticaria associated with increases in body temperature and triggers such as exercise. Trigger patterns help characterize the condition; they do not establish a diagnosis from a text description.

title: Taurine chloramine selectively regulates neutrophil degranulation
author: Kim et al.
passage: This experimental study investigated taurine chloramine and neutrophil degranulation, including myeloperoxidase and lactoferrin. A derivative acting in cells is not evidence that oral taurine treats heat-triggered hives.

title: Taurine chloramine and macrophage inflammatory mediators
author: Marcinkiewicz et al.
passage: Taurine chloramine reduced production of certain inflammatory mediators in vitro. These findings do not demonstrate a clinical effect of taurine supplementation or establish the cause of an individual response.

title: Autonomic systems
author: Ray Peat
locator: Paragraphs beginning: When nutrition and thyroid function; Parasympathetic nerves, pituitary hormones and mast cells
passage: Peat discusses estrogen-associated histamine release from ovarian mast cells and proposes that nutrition, thyroid function and environment influence autonomic signaling. This interpretive framework and ovarian observations do not establish the cause of skin hives or thyroid dysfunction in a reader.

title: Telogen effluvium
author: British Association of Dermatologists
passage: A disruption of the hair cycle can shift more follicles into a resting/shedding phase. Visible diffuse shedding may follow a trigger by months. This is not the same as pattern miniaturization, and both may occur together. Management starts with the clinical pattern and relevant history.

title: Chronic Spontaneous/Idiopathic Urticaria
author: American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology
passage: Chronic spontaneous hives often lack an identifiable cause; in most patients they are not caused by food allergy. H1 antihistamines block histamine effects and are a main treatment. Some cases associate with thyroid disease, but hives alone do not establish it. Persistent hives merit clinical evaluation.

title: Tryptophan, serotonin, and aging
author: Ray Peat
evidence: Author hypothesis; not a treatment trial
locator: Paragraph beginning: In white hair, the amount of tryptophan
passage: Peat speculates that hair loss associated with hypothyroidism, the postpartum period and certain drugs could involve serotonin excess. He also discusses serotonin, connective-tissue formation and impaired glucose oxidation. These proposed links do not prove an individual cause or show that lowering serotonin restores hair.

title: Do you have hair loss or hair shedding?
author: American Academy of Dermatology
passage: Excess shedding can follow illness, childbirth, weight loss or major stress, often with a delay of months. This differs from gradual hereditary thinning. Both can coexist, and a dermatologist can distinguish them. Do not abruptly stop a suspected medication.

title: Hair loss: Who gets and causes
author: American Academy of Dermatology
passage: Hair loss has multiple causes, including hereditary follicle changes, immune-mediated patchy loss, traction, scalp disorders, thyroid disease and nutritional deficiency. Pattern and scalp examination guide evaluation. A symptom alone cannot identify a deficiency.

title: Androgens and alopecia
author: Kaufman
passage: Androgens affect human hair differently by body site. This review discusses androgen-dependent scalp follicle miniaturization and pattern hair loss. Local follicle sensitivity matters; hair loss alone does not establish abnormal blood hormone levels.

title: Progesterone Summaries
author: Ray Peat
passage: Peat describes progesterone as involved in adaptation, stress resistance and balancing estrogen effects. This supplies context for his hormonal framework, not direct evidence for treating menstrual cramps or inferring progesterone deficiency from pain.

title: Not the female hormone, but the shock hormone
author: Ray Peat
passage: Peat discusses similarities between histamine and estrogen effects in the uterus, citing historical research. This is indirect mechanistic context; it does not establish that cramps indicate excess estrogen or that antihistamines or progesterone are appropriate treatments.

title: Dysmenorrhea: Painful Periods
author: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
passage: In primary dysmenorrhea, prostaglandins contribute to uterine muscle and blood-vessel contraction. Pain can also have secondary causes. Heat and exercise may help; medication choices require individual suitability. A period-pain framework should not be assumed for unexplained pelvic pain.

title: Primary Dysmenorrhea: Diagnosis and Therapy
author: Ferries-Rowe et al.
passage: Primary dysmenorrhea is linked to cyclooxygenase-mediated prostanoid production. Prostaglandin-related contractions and altered uterine perfusion help explain menstrual pain, without proving a generalized hormone imbalance.

title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 760: Dysmenorrhea and Endometriosis in the Adolescent
author: ACOG
passage: The guidance distinguishes primary dysmenorrhea from pelvic pathology. Persistent significant menstrual pain despite appropriate treatment warrants evaluation for secondary causes, including endometriosis. Not all painful periods imply endometriosis.

title: Ectopic Pregnancy
author: ACOG
passage: Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain or bleeding needs prompt clinical assessment. Sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, shoulder pain, weakness, dizziness or fainting can signal an emergency. An app cannot rule out ectopic pregnancy.
